tolkien.title: J. R. R. Tolkien
tolkien.text: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien (3 January 1892 – 2 September 1973) was an English writer and philologist. He was born in Bloemfontein, in the Orange Free State. He wrote The Hobbit, published in 1937, and The Lord of the Rings. From 1925 to 1945 he was Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford. J. R. R. Tolkien died in Bournemouth at the age of 81.

rainier.title: Mount Rainier
rainier.text: Mount Rainier is a large active stratovolcano in the Cascade Range of the Pacific Northwest. At 4,392 m (14,411 ft), it is the highest mountain in the U.S. state of Washington. The mountain is about 95 km southeast of Seattle. Mt. Rainier last erupted approx. 1,000 years ago, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It is not considered dormant; it is listed as a Decade Volcano. About 3.7 million people live in the area at risk from lahars.

ibuprofen.title: Ibuprofen
ibuprofen.text: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to treat pain, fever and inflammation. The usual adult dose is 200 to 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours. Adults should not take more than 1,200 mg in 24 hours without a doctor's advice. Ibuprofen is not safe in the last three months of pregnancy. It can cause stomach bleeding, especially in people over 65. Dr. Stewart Adams and his team at Boots developed it in the 1960s.

tube.title: Replacing a bicycle inner tube
tube.text: To replace an inner tube you need tyre levers and a pump. 1. Remove the wheel from the frame. 2. Use the tyre levers to lift one side of the tyre off the rim. 3. Pull out the old tube and check the inside of the tyre for thorns. 4. Inflate the new tube slightly and fit it inside the tyre. 5. Push the tyre back onto the rim and inflate it to the pressure printed on the sidewall, usually 80 to 100 psi for road tyres. Do not use a screwdriver, as it can puncture the new tube.

bs1363.title: BS 1363
bs1363.text: BS 1363 is the British standard for 13 A plugs and sockets. The plug has three rectangular pins and contains a fuse. Fuses rated at 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are common. The supply is 230 V at 50 Hz. The standard was first published in 1947. Sockets must have shutters, so that a child cannot push an object into the live contact.

australia.title: Australia
australia.text: Australia is a country made up of the mainland of the Australian continent, Tasmania and many smaller islands. Its capital is Canberra, not Sydney, which is the largest city. The population was about 27 million in 2024. Australia has six states and two major mainland territories. The head of state is the British monarch, represented by the Governor-General.

hopper.title: Grace Hopper
hopper.text: Grace Brewster Murray Hopper (1906–1992) was an American computer scientist and U.S. Navy rear admiral. She was one of the first programmers of the Harvard Mark I computer. In 1959 she helped design COBOL, a programming language for business. Rear Adm. Hopper retired from the Navy in 1986 at the age of 79. She is often credited with popularizing the term "debugging" after a moth was found in a relay.

fortworth.title: Fort Worth
fortworth.text: Fort Worth is a city in the U.S. state of Texas. It was founded in 1849 as an army outpost named Ft. Worth, after Gen. William Jenkins Worth. The city had a population of 918,915 at the 2020 census. Its Stockyards district on N. Main St. holds a cattle drive twice daily. Fort Worth lies 52 km west of Dallas.

bm.title: British Museum
bm.text: The British Museum is a public museum in London dedicated to human history, art and culture. It was established in 1753 and opened to the public in 1759. The museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. On Fridays some galleries stay open until 8:30 p.m. Admission to the permanent collection is free. It holds about 8 million objects, of which only about 80,000 are on display.

eiffel.title: Eiffel Tower
eiffel.text: The Eiffel Tower is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built it. It was completed in 1889 for the World's Fair. Including antennas, its height is 330 m. The tower weighs about 10,100 tonnes. It was the tallest man-made structure in the world until the Chrysler Building in New York was finished in 1930. Visitors can climb 674 steps to the second level.

egg.title: Boiled egg
egg.text: A boiled egg is an egg cooked in its shell in boiling water. For a soft-boiled egg, simmer it for 6 minutes; for a hard-boiled egg, simmer it for 10 to 12 minutes. Cool the egg in cold water for 2 minutes before peeling. Older eggs are easier to peel than very fresh ones. Eggs should not be boiled in a microwave, because they can explode.

tyre.title: Tyre pressure
tyre.text: Tyre pressure is the air pressure inside a tyre, measured in bar or psi. Most passenger cars need 2.2 to 2.5 bar (32 to 36 psi). The correct value is printed on a sticker inside the driver's door or in the owner's manual. Check pressure when the tyres are cold, before driving more than 3 km. Underinflated tyres wear faster and increase fuel use.

tablets.title: Water purification tablets
tablets.text: Water purification tablets release chlorine or iodine to kill germs in water. Can the water be drunk straight away? No. Wait at least 30 minutes after adding the tablet. Iodine tablets are not recommended for pregnant women. One tablet treats 1 litre of clear water; cloudy water needs two tablets.

beethoven.title: Symphony No. 5 (Beethoven)
beethoven.text: The Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, was written by Ludwig van Beethoven between 1804 and 1808. It was first performed in Vienna's Theater an der Wien in December 1808. The symphony has four movements and lasts about 30 to 40 minutes. Its opening four-note motif is one of the best-known in Western music. Beethoven's hearing was already declining when he wrote it.

grant.title: Ulysses S. Grant
grant.text: Ulysses S. Grant (1822–1885) was the 18th president of the United States, serving from 1869 to 1877. As commanding general, Gen. Grant led the Union Army to victory in the American Civil War. He was born in Point Pleasant, Ohio. Grant accepted Gen. Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865. He was 5 ft 8 in tall.

baikal.title: Lake Baikal
baikal.text: Lake Baikal is a rift lake in Siberia, Russia. It is the deepest lake in the world, with a maximum depth of 1,642 m. It holds about 23,600 cubic kilometres of fresh water, roughly 22 to 23 percent of the world's fresh surface water. The lake is 636 km long and up to 79 km wide. More than 330 rivers flow into it, but only one, the Angara, flows out. The Baikal seal is found nowhere else.

liion.title: Lithium-ion battery
liion.text: A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery in which lithium ions move between the electrodes. A typical cell has a nominal voltage of 3.6 V. Most phone batteries keep about 80 percent of their capacity after 500 full charge cycles. Do not charge a swollen battery. Store them at 40 to 60 percent charge in a cool place if unused for months. Lithium-ion cells were first sold by Sony in 1991.

voyager.title: Rutan Voyager
voyager.text: The Rutan Voyager was the first aircraft to fly around the world without stopping or refuelling. It was flown by Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager. The flight took off from Edwards Air Force Base in California on 14 December 1986 and lasted 9 days, 3 minutes and 44 seconds. The aircraft covered 42,432 km. Its wingspan was 33.8 m. Burt Rutan, Dick's brother, designed it.

tomato.title: Tomato plant care
tomato.text: Tomatoes need at least 6 hours of direct sun a day. Water them deeply two or three times a week rather than a little every day. Tomato leaves are not edible; they contain small amounts of toxic alkaloids. Plant seedlings 45 to 60 cm apart. Most varieties ripen 60 to 80 days after transplanting.

stlouis.title: St. Louis
stlouis.text: St. Louis is an independent city in the U.S. state of Missouri, on the Mississippi River. It was founded in 1764 by French fur traders Pierre Laclède and Auguste Chouteau. The Gateway Arch, completed in 1965, is 192 m tall. The city hosted the 1904 Summer Olympics and the World's Fair. Its population was 301,578 in 2020.

measles.title: Measles
measles.text: Measles is a highly contagious disease caused by the measles virus. Symptoms usually appear 10 to 12 days after exposure and include fever, cough and a rash. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective. The vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy. In 2023 there were an estimated 107,500 measles deaths worldwide, mostly among children under 5.

ggb.title: Golden Gate Bridge
ggb.text: The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate strait in San Francisco, California. It opened in 1937. The main span is 1,280 m long. Its towers rise 227 m above the water. The chief engineer was Joseph Strauss, but much of the design was by Charles Ellis and Leon Moisseiff. The bridge is painted International Orange.

bread.title: Basic white bread
bread.text: Mix 500 g of strong white flour, 7 g of dried yeast, 10 g of salt and 300 ml of warm water. Knead the dough for 10 minutes until smooth. Leave it to rise for about 1 hour, until doubled in size. Bake at 220 °C for 30 to 35 minutes. The loaf is done when it sounds hollow when tapped underneath.

curie.title: Marie Curie
curie.text: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934) was a Polish and naturalised-French physicist and chemist. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering polonium and radium. She died of aplastic anaemia, probably caused by radiation exposure.

bison.title: American bison
bison.text: The American bison is a species of bison native to North America. By 1889 fewer than 1,000 remained in the U.S. Today they number about 31,000 in public herds. An adult bull can weigh up to 1,000 kg and stand 1.8 m at the shoulder. Bison can run at 55 km/h. They are not domesticated cattle, and they can be dangerous to visitors.

hands.title: Hand washing
hands.text: Hand washing is cleaning one's hands with soap and water to remove germs. Wash for at least 20 seconds, i.e. about the time it takes to hum "Happy Birthday" twice. Dry hands with a clean towel or air dryer. Alcohol-based sanitisers (e.g. gels with at least 60% alcohol) can be used when soap is not available. Sanitisers do not work well on visibly dirty hands.

apollo.title: Apollo 11
apollo.text: Apollo 11 was the first crewed mission to land on the Moon. Commander Neil Armstrong and lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin landed the Eagle on 20 July 1969. Armstrong stepped onto the surface six hours later. He was joined by Aldrin 19 minutes later. Michael Collins stayed in lunar orbit in the command module Columbia. The mission returned to Earth on 24 July 1969.

holmes.title: Sherlock Holmes Museum
holmes.text: The Sherlock Holmes Museum is a privately run museum in London. It is at 221B Baker St. The building was a lodging house from 1860 to 1936. Tickets cost approx. £16 for adults. It is open 9:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. every day except Christmas Day. The museum is not connected with the Sherlock Holmes stories' author, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

torque.title: Torque wrench
torque.text: A torque wrench is a tool used to apply a specific torque to a fastener such as a nut or bolt. Typical car wheel nuts are tightened to 110 to 140 N·m (80 to 100 lb·ft). Click-type wrenches, beam wrenches, etc. are all common. Always set a click wrench back to its lowest setting after use. Do not use a torque wrench to loosen bolts. Accuracy is usually within ±4% of the set value.

mlk.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
mlk.text: Martin Luther King Jr. (January 15, 1929 – April 4, 1968) was an American Baptist minister and civil rights leader. He was born in Atlanta, Georgia. King led the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955. He delivered the "I Have a Dream" speech at the March on Washington in 1963. In 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize. He was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.
